title: Generative engine optimization (GEO): how firms get cited
h1: Generative engine optimization: how a firm gets found and cited in AI answers
desc: GEO makes a firm easy for ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Google's AI answers to find and quote: answer-first pages, consistent facts, open crawl access.
lead: Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is the work of making a firm's website easy for AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Google's AI answers to find, read and quote correctly. It rests on plain habits: pages that answer the question in their first lines, one consistent set of facts about the firm, structured data, and letting the assistants' crawlers in. There is no secret ranking formula.
short: GEO is visibility in AI answers: being found, understood and quoted accurately.
Pages that answer first, in plain words, are the easiest for an assistant to quote.
The firm's name, services and location should read the same everywhere they appear.
Structured data and open crawl access help assistants read the site; nothing guarantees a citation.

sections.h2: What is generative engine optimization?
body: Generative engine optimization is the practice of preparing a website so that AI assistants can use it as a source. When someone asks an assistant which firm handles a certain kind of work, or how a service works, the assistant writes an answer and often names the pages it drew on. GEO is about being one of those pages, and being described correctly when it happens.

It is not a replacement for search engine optimization. Many assistants look things up through a search index or their own crawler before they answer, so the basics of SEO still apply: a site that loads, pages that can be read, and content that matches what people ask. GEO adds attention to how an answer is lifted from a page and repeated elsewhere.

The two also share an audience. The person who reads an assistant's answer and then clicks through to the firm's site should find the same facts, in the same words, on the page itself. A site that serves that reader well tends to serve the assistant well too.

sections.h2: How do AI assistants choose what to quote?
body: No assistant publishes a full list of what makes it cite one page over another, and claims of exact ranking factors should be treated with caution. What is widely understood is the general shape of the process. The assistant retrieves pages that seem relevant to the question, reads them, and writes a summary. A page that states a clear answer in plain sentences is easier to summarize accurately than one that buries it.

That leads to a practical rule rather than a trick. If a page would be a good answer for a careful human reader, it stands a better chance of being a good source for an assistant. Vague pages, pages that say the same thing in several contradicting ways, and pages that hide their text behind scripts give the assistant less to work with.

sections.h2: What does an answer-first page look like?
body: An answer-first page puts the answer to its main question at the top, then explains. It is written for the person asking, not for a search engine. These are the habits that make a page easy to quote:
The question the page answers appears in the title, in words a client would use.
The first paragraph gives the direct answer in two or three sentences.
Headings are phrased as the questions people actually ask.
Paragraphs are short, and each one makes a single point.
Lists are used for steps, options and requirements, so they can be lifted whole.
A short summary and a few common questions close the page.
This article follows the same pattern. None of it is unusual writing advice; it simply removes the work an assistant, or a busy reader, would otherwise have to do.

sections.h2: Why do entity clarity and consistent facts matter?
body: To an assistant, a firm is an entity: a named thing with properties such as what it does, where it works and how to reach it. If those properties read differently from one place to another, the assistant has to guess, and guesses produce wrong descriptions. Entity clarity means stating the facts once, plainly, and repeating them the same way everywhere.
The places to check are usually the ones nobody has looked at in a while:
The firm's own website, including the footer and the contact page.
Its business profile on Google Maps and any directory listings.
Company pages on LinkedIn and other social networks.
Short bios on Substack, Instagram or industry sites.
Old pages or press mentions that describe services the firm no longer offers.

Correcting these is mostly copying and retyping, which is exactly the kind of chore that gets skipped. It is also the part of GEO that most directly affects whether an answer describes the firm correctly.

sections.h2: Which technical steps let assistants read the site?
body: Good writing is wasted if an assistant cannot reach it. A few technical checks matter more than any others:

Crawl access: the site's robots.txt file should not block the crawlers the firm wants to be read by, such as GPTBot and OAI-SearchBot for OpenAI, ClaudeBot for Anthropic and PerplexityBot for Perplexity.
Readable text: the main content should be in the page itself, not loaded later by scripts that some crawlers do not run.
Structured data: schema.org markup that states who the firm is, what it offers and which questions a page answers.
A sitemap that lists every page worth reading.
A plain-text summary such as llms.txt, a proposed convention that some tools read. It is useful, but not an official standard.
Each of these removes an obstacle. None of them forces an assistant to cite the firm, and it is worth being wary of anyone who promises otherwise.

sections.h2: How does Loose Ends approach GEO for a firm?
body: The studio treats GEO as part of building the site, not as a separate campaign. The firm's facts are written once, in one place, and the page, the structured data and the plain-text summary are generated from that same source, so they cannot drift apart. Pages are written answer first, in the firm's own voice, without filler written for machines.

The work usually starts by reading the existing site the way an assistant would: what it can reach, what it can understand, and where the facts disagree. From there the fixes are ranked by how much they change, and the firm decides what to do first. Loose Ends offers a free one-page review of where the firm loses time, with no call required, and it is the simplest place to start.

faq.q: Is GEO different from SEO?
faq.a: GEO builds on SEO rather than replacing it. SEO is about being found in search results; GEO adds attention to how assistants read a page and repeat its answer.

faq.q: Can a firm guarantee being cited by ChatGPT or Perplexity?
faq.a: No. Nobody outside those companies controls what their assistants cite. A firm can only make its pages easy to reach, easy to read and consistent.

faq.q: Should a firm block AI crawlers?
faq.a: That is a business decision. Blocking them protects content from being read, but it also means the assistants have less to go on when they describe the firm.

faq.q: Does llms.txt help with GEO?
faq.a: It can help tools that read it, and it costs little to maintain. It is a proposed convention, not an official standard, so it should not be the only step.

title: Structured data and llms.txt: what each one does
h1: Structured data and llms.txt: what each one does for a firm's website
desc: Structured data tells search engines and assistants what a page is about; llms.txt gives them a plain-text summary. Neither guarantees ranking or citation.
lead: Structured data is code in a web page that states, in a fixed vocabulary from schema.org, who the firm is, what it offers and which questions the page answers. llms.txt is a plain-text summary of a site placed at its root for AI assistants to read. Both make a site easier to understand; neither guarantees a ranking or a citation.
short: Structured data describes a page in a vocabulary machines read without guessing.
Organization or ProfessionalService, FAQPage and Article cover most of what a firm needs.
llms.txt is a proposed convention, not an official standard, and support for it varies.
Both should be generated from the same source as the page, so they never disagree with it.

sections.h2: What is structured data?
body: Structured data is a block of code, usually in a format called JSON-LD, placed in a page's HTML. It is not shown to visitors. It describes what the page contains using types and properties defined at schema.org, a shared vocabulary supported by the major search engines.

A sentence on a page such as a description of services can be read in many ways. The same information in structured data is labelled: this is the firm's name, this is its address, this is a service it offers, this is a question and this is its answer. Search engines and other tools can read those labels without interpreting the prose.

For a firm, the useful part is precision. A page might mention several cities, several services and several people; the markup states which city the firm is based in, which services it sells and who publishes the page. That removes guesswork for any tool that reads it, including the crawlers that feed AI assistants.

sections.h2: Which schema.org types matter for a firm's website?
body: Schema.org defines hundreds of types, but a firm's site rarely needs more than a handful. These are the ones that do most of the work:
Organization, or the more specific ProfessionalService: the firm's name, description, website, contact details, the area it serves and the services it offers.
FAQPage: the questions on a page and their answers, as pairs.
Article: a piece of writing, with its headline, description, author or publisher and the date it was published or updated.
WebSite and BreadcrumbList: the site's name and where a page sits within it.

One caution about FAQPage. Google now shows FAQ results in search for only a limited set of sites, so the markup should not be added in the hope of a visual change in results. It is still a clear, machine-readable statement of what a page answers.

sections.h2: What is llms.txt?
body: llms.txt is a proposal, published in 2024, for a plain-text file at the root of a website, written in Markdown, that summarizes the site for large language models. It typically opens with the site's name and a one-line description, then lists the main sections with short notes and links.

The idea is that an assistant reading a site, or a person pasting it into one, gets a clean summary instead of navigation menus, scripts and layout. It is a proposed convention, not an official standard, and there is no public commitment from the main assistant makers to read it. It is cheap to produce, which is why it is worth having, but it should be treated as a courtesy rather than a lever.

A good llms.txt is short and factual. It says what the firm does, for whom, and where the detail lives on the site. It repeats the same facts as the pages, in the same words, and links to them rather than replacing them.

sections.h2: What do structured data and llms.txt not guarantee?
body: Both are often sold as more than they are. It helps to be clear about the limits:
Neither one guarantees a higher position in search results.
Neither one guarantees that ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity or Google's AI answers will cite the firm.
Structured data that contradicts the visible page can be ignored, and in search it can count against the site.
An llms.txt file that is out of date gives assistants the wrong facts, which is worse than giving them none.
What they do reliably is remove ambiguity. A firm that states its facts clearly, in the page, in the markup and in the summary, gives every reader, human or not, the same answer.

sections.h2: How does this site use structured data and llms.txt?
body: The Loose Ends site describes the studio as a ProfessionalService in its structured data, with its services and the area it works in. The questions section on the page and the FAQPage markup are generated from the same list, so the questions a visitor reads are exactly the ones the markup states. Blog articles such as this one are described as BlogPosting, a kind of Article.

The site also publishes an llms.txt file. It is not written by hand. It is generated from the same lists that produce the page: the services, the cases and the questions. When a line of wording changes, the page, the structured data and the summary change together. That single source is the main safeguard, because the most common fault in this area is not missing markup but markup that has quietly fallen out of step with the page.

sections.h2: How should a firm add them without making mistakes?
body: The safest approach is to treat structured data and llms.txt as outputs of the website, not as separate documents someone has to remember to update. In practice that means:
Keep the firm's facts in one place and generate the page, the markup and the summary from it.
Mark up only what the page actually shows; never add questions or services that are not visible.
Check the markup with Google's Rich Results Test and the Schema Markup Validator after each change.
Review llms.txt whenever services, cases or contact details change.

For a firm whose site was built without this, the first step is usually a short audit of what the markup says against what the page says. Loose Ends offers a free one-page review of where the firm loses time, with no call required, and it is the simplest place to start.

faq.q: Does structured data improve rankings?
faq.a: Not directly. It helps search engines understand a page and can make it eligible for certain search features, but it is not a ranking boost in itself.

faq.q: Is llms.txt an official standard?
faq.a: No. It is a proposed convention from 2024. Some tools read it, and there is no guarantee that any particular assistant does.

faq.q: Should a firm use Organization or ProfessionalService?
faq.a: ProfessionalService is a more specific kind of Organization for firms that sell services. Either is valid; the more specific type says a little more.

faq.q: Can structured data be added to an existing site?
faq.a: Yes. It is added to the page code without changing how the page looks. The care is in keeping it in step with the visible content afterwards.

title: Content system: one idea into an article and a week of posts
h1: A content system that turns one idea into a researched article and a week of posts
desc: A content system turns one idea into a researched article and a week of posts for Substack, LinkedIn and Instagram, every figure checked against a source.
lead: A content system is a set routine, partly automated, that takes one idea from the firm and turns it into a researched article and a week of posts for Substack, LinkedIn and Instagram. Every figure is checked against a named source before anything goes out, the wording follows the firm's own voice, and a person approves each piece before it is published.
short: One idea feeds an article and a week of posts, instead of a fresh start every day.
Every figure carries a named source; a figure without one is cut, not guessed.
The firm's voice is written down once and applied to every draft.
The system drafts and schedules; a person approves before anything is published.

sections.h2: What is a content system, and how is it different from a content calendar?
body: A content calendar says what should go out and when. A content system also does much of the work in between: the research, the first drafts, the versions for each platform and the scheduling. The calendar is a plan; the system is the routine that fills it.

The difference shows up in the chores that usually stall publishing. Someone has to find sources, copy figures into a draft, rewrite the same point for three platforms, resize images, and chase whoever needs to sign off. A content system takes on that preparation so the team spends its time on the parts only it can do: the idea, the judgement and the final word.

sections.h2: How does one idea become a researched article?
body: The process starts with something the firm already knows: a question clients keep asking, a change in its field, a lesson from recent work. From there the system works through a fixed sequence:
The idea is written down in a few lines by someone at the firm.
The system gathers sources on the subject and lists them, with links, for the team to see.
It drafts an outline, then an article, written in the firm's voice and structured to answer the question directly.
Every claim and figure in the draft is tied to the source it came from.
A person at the firm reads, edits and approves the article.
The article is the anchor. Everything published that week points back to it, which keeps the message consistent and gives readers somewhere to go for the full argument.

The research step is also where the system saves the most repetitive work. Instead of someone opening tabs, copying passages into a document and retyping references, the sources arrive already listed, each with its link and the passage that matters. The team's time goes into deciding whether a source is good enough, not into collecting it.

sections.h2: How is every figure checked before it goes out?
body: Figures are where AI-written content most often goes wrong. A language model can produce a number that sounds right and has no source at all. The system is built so that this cannot pass quietly.

Each figure in a draft is stored alongside a named source: the publication or organization, the document, and a link. Before a draft reaches the approver, the system checks that every figure has one. A figure without a source is flagged and removed, never filled in with an estimate. The approver sees the sources beside the text, so checking a claim means opening a link, not starting a search.
This makes the firm slower to repeat a figure it has not verified, which is the point. A single wrong number in a published post costs more trust than a post without numbers.

sections.h2: How does the article become a week of posts?
body: Once the article is approved, the system prepares a week of shorter pieces from it, each written for the platform it will appear on. A typical set looks like this:
Substack: the full article as a newsletter issue, with a short introduction for subscribers.
LinkedIn: several posts, each built around a single point from the article, written to be read in the feed.
Instagram: captions and simple carousel text drawn from the clearest points, paired with images in the firm's visual style.
A schedule that spreads the posts across the week, ready to be queued once approved.
Each post can stand on its own, but each also links back to the article. Nothing new is claimed in the posts that the article does not already support with a source.
This is also what makes the week manageable. The team approves one article and one batch of posts, rather than facing a blank page every morning and deciding, again, what to say and where.

sections.h2: How does the system keep the firm's own voice?
body: A generic assistant writes in a generic voice. To avoid that, the firm's voice is written down once as a short guide: how it addresses readers, words it uses and words it never uses, sentence length, and examples of past writing the firm is proud of. The guide is given to the system with every draft.

The approver's edits are part of the routine too. When the same correction keeps coming back, it goes into the guide, so the next draft starts closer to how the firm actually writes. Over time the drafts need less editing, and the editing that remains is about substance rather than tone.

The visual side follows the same principle. Images for Instagram and LinkedIn are prepared in the firm's colors and type, from templates designed once, so a week of posts looks like it came from the same firm without anyone resizing and recoloring each image by hand.

sections.h2: Who approves, and what does the team still do?
body: Nothing is published without a person's approval. The system drafts, checks sources and prepares the schedule; someone at the firm reads each piece, edits it and approves it, and only then is it queued on Substack, LinkedIn or Instagram. The firm chooses the ideas, makes the judgement calls and owns the result.

Loose Ends has built a system of this kind and sets it up inside the tools a firm already uses, connected to its own accounts, with training and a named owner for the routine at handover. Loose Ends offers a free one-page review of where the firm loses time, with no call required, and it is the simplest place to start.

faq.q: Does the system publish posts automatically?
faq.a: It prepares and schedules them, but a person approves every piece first. Nothing goes out on the system's judgement alone.

faq.q: What happens if a source cannot be found for a figure?
faq.a: The figure is removed. The system flags it for the approver and never replaces it with an estimate.

faq.q: Which platforms does it work with?
faq.a: The routine described here covers Substack, LinkedIn and Instagram. Other channels can be added when a firm uses them.

faq.q: Will the posts sound like AI?
faq.a: The drafts follow a written guide to the firm's voice, and a person edits each one. The guide improves as the same corrections are added to it.

title: AI assistant for journalists: an editorial week around video
h1: An AI assistant for journalists, set up around an editorial week with video at the centre
desc: An AI assistant for journalists can take on the repeated preparation around video, from research notes to captions, while editorial judgement stays human.
lead: An AI assistant for a journalist works best when it is set up around the journalist's own editorial week rather than the software's defaults. It can take on the repeated preparation around reporting and video production: research notes, transcripts, outlines, captions and descriptions. The choice of story, the framing, the verification and the final cut stay with the journalist.
short: The assistant is shaped around the editorial week, not the other way round.
Repeated preparation is automated so it runs the same way every time.
Story choice, framing, verification and the final cut remain editorial judgement.
Anything sent to a source, a client or an editor is approved by the journalist first.

sections.h2: What can an AI assistant do in a journalist's editorial week?
body: Most journalists already use an AI assistant for something: a summary, a headline idea, a rough translation. Used that way, it starts from nothing each time, and the results vary with how the request happens to be worded. Most of what the assistant can do goes unused.

Set up properly, the assistant knows the shape of the week. It knows which tasks come up on which days, what each one needs, and the format the result should take. The journalist asks for the task by name, and it runs the same way as last time, with the same structure and the same checks. The value is less in any single answer than in the routine becoming dependable.

A typical week has a recognizable rhythm: planning the stories, research and interviews, writing and scripting, shooting and editing, then publishing and answering what comes back. Each part has its own repeated chores, and each can be given a routine that the assistant runs on request.

sections.h2: What should be automated, and what stays editorial judgement?
body: The line is drawn by asking whether a task is preparation or decision. Preparation can be handed to the assistant; decisions stay with the journalist.
Tasks that suit the assistant:
Turning interview recordings into transcripts and pulling out the passages that bear on the story.
Gathering background on a subject and listing the sources it came from.
Drafting outlines, scripts and shot lists from the journalist's notes.
Writing first versions of captions, video descriptions and post text for each platform.
Filing material, naming files consistently and keeping notes in one place.
Tasks that stay editorial judgement:
Choosing the story and the angle.
Verifying facts, quotes and footage.
Deciding what goes in the final cut and what is left out.
Anything said to a source, and anything published under the journalist's name.

sections.h2: How does video production sit at the centre of the setup?
body: For a journalist working in video, the week bends around production. Research feeds a script, the script feeds the shoot, the footage feeds the edit, and the edit feeds publishing on several platforms. Each hand-off involves text that has to be prepared: notes become a script, a script becomes a shot list, a finished video needs a title, a description, captions and posts.

That text is where the assistant earns its place. It does not edit the video; that remains the work of the journalist or an editor. It prepares everything around the video, in the formats each stage needs, so the journalist moves from one stage to the next without retyping or copying between documents.

Consistency matters here as much as saving effort. When captions, descriptions and file names follow the same pattern every week, the archive stays searchable, and finding an old clip or a past interview takes a search rather than an afternoon of digging.

sections.h2: Case: a journalist working in video
body: Loose Ends set up the AI assistant of a journalist who works in video. The assistant was arranged around his editorial week, not around the software's defaults. The tasks he repeats now run the same way every time, with video production at the centre of the setup. The work was delivered in 2026.

The approach is the one described in this article: map the week, separate preparation from decision, and give each repeated task a fixed form so the result is consistent. The journalist keeps every editorial decision; the assistant keeps the routine.
What changed is less visible than a new tool but more useful day to day. A task that used to depend on remembering how it was done last time now has a written form, and the assistant follows it.

sections.h2: How is the assistant connected to the journalist's own material?
body: An assistant is only as useful as what it can see. Connecting it to the journalist's own tools means it can read the notes, files and calendar it needs, instead of relying on whatever is pasted into a chat.

Claude does this through connectors built on MCP, the Model Context Protocol, an open standard introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 for connecting AI assistants to tools and data. Typical connections for a journalist include:
Email and calendar, to see what is scheduled and what needs answering.
A document store or drive, where scripts, notes and transcripts live.
A notes or task tool that holds the story list.
The publishing platforms, so post drafts can be prepared in the right format.
Access is set deliberately. The assistant can read what it needs to prepare drafts; anything that would be sent to someone outside waits for the journalist's approval.

sections.h2: How does a journalist or newsroom start?
body: The starting point is a plain account of one ordinary week: what happens each day, what gets repeated, and where time goes to copying, retyping and chasing. From that, the tasks worth turning into routines become obvious, and so do the ones that should stay as they are. It is better to start with a few routines that run well than with many that run sometimes, and to add more once the first ones have proved themselves in a real week.

Loose Ends sets up the assistant, connects it to the tools in use, writes each routine down, and hands it over with training so the journalist can adjust it later. Loose Ends offers a free one-page review of where the firm loses time, with no call required, and it is the simplest place to start.

faq.q: Can an AI assistant edit video for a journalist?
faq.a: The setup described here does not hand the edit to the assistant. It prepares the text around the video, such as scripts, shot lists, captions and descriptions, and the journalist or an editor makes the cut.

faq.q: Does the assistant publish anything on its own?
faq.a: No. It prepares drafts, and the journalist approves anything before it is published or sent to anyone.

faq.q: Which AI assistant is this built on?
faq.a: Claude is a common choice because of its connectors built on MCP, but the same approach applies to other assistants that can connect to a journalist's tools.

faq.q: Is this only for independent journalists?
faq.a: No. The same method works for a newsroom team: map the week, decide what is preparation and what is judgement, and give each repeated task a fixed form.

title: Brand identity for a guesthouse, drawn from the building
h1: Brand identity for a guesthouse, drawn from the house's own materials
desc: A guesthouse brand identity drawn from the building's tiles, doors and objects, carried through a bilingual website and the printed pieces guests hold.
lead: A brand identity for a guesthouse is strongest when it is drawn from the building itself: its tiles, doors, ironwork and everyday objects. Those motifs become the mark, the patterns and the colors, and they are carried through a bilingual website and every printed piece a guest holds, from the room card to the menu. The guest then recognizes the house in every part of the stay.
short: The house already has a visual language; the identity is drawn from it by hand.
Tiles, doors and objects become the mark, patterns and palette.
The website treats both languages as equal, not one as a translation of the other.
Printed pieces carry the identity into the guest's hands during the stay.

sections.h2: What does it mean to build an identity from a building's materials?
body: Many guesthouses use an identity that could belong to any hotel: a tidy logo, a neutral typeface, a stock palette. It is inoffensive and forgettable. A house with history already has a visual language of its own, in its floors, its doorways and the objects that have collected in it over time.

Building the identity from those materials means looking closely at the house first and drawing what is there. The patterns, shapes and colors that result belong to that building and no other. When a guest arrives, the place matches what they saw online, and the identity feels like part of the house rather than something applied to it.

It is also practical. A guesthouse cannot compete with large hotels on scale, but it can offer something they cannot: a specific place with its own character. An identity taken from the building puts that character at the front of every page and every piece of paper.

sections.h2: Case: a nineteenth-century maison d'hôte in La Marsa
body: Loose Ends designed the identity for a maison d'hôte, a guesthouse, in La Marsa, set in a nineteenth-century house. The identity was drawn by hand from the house's own tiles, doors and objects.

It was carried through a website in French and English and through the printed pieces guests hold, from the room card to the table d'hôte menu. The identity and the printed pieces have been delivered; the website is in development.

sections.h2: How is an identity drawn from tiles, doors and objects?
body: The method is close observation followed by careful drawing. It moves through a few stages:
Survey the house: photograph and sketch the tiles, door panels, ironwork, plaster details and objects that recur.
Choose the motifs that are most characteristic and that still read clearly at small sizes.
Redraw them by hand, simplifying each one until it works as a line on paper and on a screen.
Take the palette from the materials themselves, the glaze of a tile, painted wood, stone.
Build a small system: a main mark, secondary patterns, a palette and type, with rules for how they combine.
Drawing by hand matters. A traced or generated pattern looks mechanical next to the real tiles. A drawn one keeps the slight irregularity that makes the original feel made by people.
The result is documented in a short guide, so that anyone who later prints a new card, updates the website or designs a sign can use the identity correctly without starting again.

sections.h2: How does the identity carry through a bilingual website?
body: For a guesthouse, the website does the work of a front desk before the guest arrives: it shows the rooms, answers questions and takes the first step towards a booking. In a bilingual site, both languages need equal standing. A guest reading in English should not feel they are on a translated afterthought of the French site, or the other way round.
In practice that means:
Each language is written and checked by a person, not left to machine translation.
Layouts are designed for both, since the same sentence runs to different lengths in French and English.
Practical details, such as arrival times, directions and house rules, read the same in both languages.
The drawn motifs, palette and type carry across every page, so the site feels like the house.
Enquiries from the site can feed into the house's own email or booking tool, with replies drafted for the owner to check and approve before anything is sent to a guest.

sections.h2: Which printed pieces do guests hold?
body: Print is where the identity is touched rather than seen. A guest handles these pieces during the stay, often more than once, and they shape how the house is remembered. A guesthouse's printed set can include:
A room card with the room name, practical details and a welcome.
The table d'hôte menu, for meals shared at the house.
Notes on the house, the neighborhood and how to get around.
Stationery for letters, receipts and small messages.

Each piece follows the same system: the drawn motifs, the palette from the house, and type chosen to read well in both languages. Paper and printing are chosen with the same care, because a guest notices the weight of a card in the hand.

Like the website, the printed pieces are bilingual where guests need them to be. A menu or a room card that serves guests in two languages has to be laid out for both from the start, not translated into a corner afterwards.

sections.h2: How does a guesthouse or hotel start?
body: The first step is a walk through the house with fresh eyes, noting what is distinctive and what guests already comment on. That list is the raw material for the identity, and it often includes details the owners have stopped noticing because they pass them every day. The second is a plain inventory of what guests see and hold: the website, the booking messages, the room cards, the menu, the signage.

Loose Ends works from both lists, drawing the identity and then carrying it through each piece, so that print and website are designed together rather than one after the other. The house's owners approve each stage before the next one begins. Loose Ends offers a free one-page review of where the firm loses time, with no call required, and it is the simplest place to start.

faq.q: Why draw the identity by hand rather than use a template?
faq.a: A hand-drawn identity taken from the house belongs to that house alone. A template could belong to any hotel, and guests can tell the difference.

faq.q: Does a bilingual website need two separate designs?
faq.a: No. It needs one design that works for both languages, with room for the differences in sentence length and wording.

faq.q: Which printed pieces matter most for a guesthouse?
faq.a: The ones guests hold during the stay, such as the room card and the menu, since they are handled more than once and shape how the house is remembered.

faq.q: Can the website take bookings?
faq.a: It can lead to the house's own booking tool or enquiry form. Replies to guests are drafted for the owner to approve before they are sent.
